A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiDA despite the changed title and presentation. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments on GTAv-to-Cityscapes and SYNTHIA-to-Cityscapes, component ablations, sensitivity studies and reconstruction analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Cityscapes-to-ACDC results, computational measurements and revised domain-bridging analyses.

M1.justification: The degradation processes, time-conditioned diffusion encoder, residual feature fusion, losses and ordinary inference procedure remain unchanged. The memory-friendly DiDA(gtime) discussed in v2 Appendix E already appears as the encoder-ablation configuration in v1 Table 4; it is not a newly introduced method.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cityscapes-to-ACDC adaptation covering fog, night, rain and snow, extending evaluation from synthetic-to-real transfer to real-world clear-to-adverse conditions. Both original synthetic-to-Cityscapes tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds ADFormer and CoPT to both synthetic-to-real comparisons (Tables 3–4), and ADVENT, DANNet and FREST to the new ACDC comparison (Table 5). This substantially expands the comparator coverage while retaining the original host methods and plug-in comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 Appendix H replaces feature-based t-SNE/MMD evaluation with absolute mIoU and UDA-to-oracle performance ratios across degradation levels. Oracle, source-only and DAFormer models are trained separately at each level, whereas DiDA is trained once. Appendix E additionally measures memory and training time. The original benchmarks retain their stated training budgets and inference schemes.

E4.justification: The domain-bridging investigation changes substantially: v1 Section 4.3.7 examines feature clustering and discrepancy, while v2 Appendix H compares supervised and adaptation performance under degradation. v2 also adds an efficiency analysis of full DiDA and the existing gtime variant. Most component, parameter, schedule and reconstruction analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's checklist explicitly acknowledges that error bars are omitted because of computational expense, without introducing a different statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds ACDC results, including 59.1, 70.7 and 72.1 mIoU for DiDA with DAFormer, HRDA and MIC, respectively, plus computational measurements and new degradation-performance curves. MIC baseline scores change from 75.9 to 75.5 on GTA with the Transformer and from 62.8 to 62.4 on SYNTHIA with the CNN, marked as reproduced results. Corresponding DiDA scores remain unchanged; the enlarged margins are not cross-version DiDA performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 adds an Attribute Loss and Time Step proposition absent from v1, connecting attribute-loss thresholds and stochastic dominance to diffusion time. It is attributed to prior work and supplied without a local proof. The existing method equations and degradation formulations remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now explicitly identify self-training's lack of domain-shared feature modeling as the central gap, whereas v1 foregrounds limitations of translation- and mixing-based bridges. The main claims about degradation-based bridging, semantic-shift compensation, plug-in compatibility and improved segmentation performance remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops an interpretation involving early loss of domain-specific attributes, later loss of semantic attributes and distribution overlap as a shared-domain prior. Appendix D attributes weather-transfer gains to similarities between degradation and weather corruption. Appendices E and N add substantive qualifications about training overhead, resource constraints and manually selected degradation operations.

D1.justification: v2 adds per-method memory, iteration-time and total-training-time information in Table 6, but removes v1's explicit resizing, cropping, augmentation and dataset-download details. Most hyperparameters remain. The abstract changes code availability from promised to available, while the checklist still promises release upon acceptance, leaving the reported release status inconsistent.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through causal/disentangled representation learning, diffusion attribute-loss theory, recent UDA methods and label-efficient segmentation literature. Some earlier translation and ClassMix citations disappear. The original domain-bridging related-work discussion is largely retained in Appendix M rather than removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces a theoretical-insight subsection and reorganizes the algorithm, degradation derivations and many diagnostic analyses into thematic appendices, alongside a conference checklist. The title, author list and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document from two-column to single-column presentation and converts rotated full-page result tables into compact upright tables. Figure 1 is substantially redesigned, the domain-bridging plots are replaced, and ACDC and efficiency tables are added. Numerous retained figures and tables are resized, recolored or relocated.

improvement.justification: The adverse-weather evaluation strengthens evidence beyond v1's synthetic-to-real settings, while the efficiency measurements and explicit limitations make practical tradeoffs clearer. These benefits support a net improvement, tempered by omitted preprocessing details, obsolete equation references in the relocated Algorithm 1 and conflicting code-release statements. The added theoretical proposition also lacks the local proof claimed by the checklist, limiting the gain in theoretical rigor.
